overview.title: 📖 Overview: Timing, Discharges, and a New Mishna
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 21a–21b
overview.hebrewSource: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר: בְּהֵמָה גַּסָּה שֶׁשָּׁפְעָה חֲרָרַת דָּם, הֲרֵי זוֹ תִּקָּבֵר, וּפְטוּרָה מִן הַבְּכוֹרָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf finishes the goat-triplets tithe puzzle by adding a fourth possible explanation for the dispute between the baraita's first tanna and Rabbi Shimon: whether an animal too young to be sacrificed (מְחוּסַּר זְמַן) may still enter the pen to be counted for the tithe. The Gemara then works out where that halakha itself comes from, testing an analogy to the firstborn against one to ordinary sacrifices before settling on a verbal analogy Rabbi Shimon employs. A short discussion defines what physically counts as the murky discharge that exempts a future offspring, and Rav Ḥisda's related question about how long fetal formation takes in an animal is left unresolved. The Gemara then asks what happens when an animal is purchased from a fellow Jew rather than a gentile, weighing three opinions before the mishna turns to a new case: a large animal that expels a mass of congealed blood.

slides.title: 🐐 Tanna Kama vs. Rabbi Shimon: Four Explanations
slides.subtitle: The second-generation goats discharge at the start of month seven — did they still give birth in time?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Explanation 1 (Ze'eiri's rule): the first tanna accepts that a discharge blocks pregnancy for 30 days, pushing any birth into year two; Rabbi Shimon rejects Ze'eiri, allowing a year-one birth
2️⃣ Explanation 2 (premature birth): both accept Ze'eiri, but dispute whether an animal can give birth prematurely (מְקוּטָּעִין) — the first tanna says no, Rabbi Shimon says yes
3️⃣ Explanation 3 (part of a day): both reject premature birth, but dispute whether part of a day counts as a whole day — the first tanna says no, Rabbi Shimon says yes
4️⃣ Explanation 4 (new): all agree part of a day counts as whole — instead they dispute whether an animal too young to be sacrificed (מְחוּסַּר זְמַן) may even enter the pen to be tithed at all

callout.label: Pattern:
callout.text: Each 'if you wish, say instead' isolates one more variable, the same technique used on 20a–20b for a different dispute.

slides.title: 📜 Where Does 'Mechusar Zman Enters the Pen' Come From?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, in Rabbi Shimon's name: it does — but why?

boxes.title: Parallels to the Firstborn (chosen first)
items: Cannot be redeemed even once blemished
A blemish does not prevent consecration
A substitute animal is never sacrificed

boxes.title: Parallels to Ordinary Sacrifices (rejected)
items: Sanctified through human action, not intrinsically
Not among the gifts given to a priest
Begins life as an ordinary, unremarkable animal

boxes.title: Rabbi Shimon's Real Source
items: Not an analogy of traits at all — a verbal analogy (גְּזֵרָה שָׁוָה)
'Whatsoever passes under the rod' (יַעֲבוֹר, Leviticus 27:32, tithe)

callout.label: Twist:
callout.text: After the Gemara argues both ways about which comparison fits better, it concludes the real derivation was never about shared traits at all.

slides.title: 🩸 What Exactly Is a 'Murky Discharge'?
slides.subtitle: Defining the sign that exempts a future offspring from firstborn status
rows: A discharge indicating the animal absorbed or suppressed a fetus within the womb
The discharge must be shown to a knowledgeable shepherd, familiar with the different kinds of discharge — not a Torah scholar
Fetal formation in a woman takes 40 days — how long does it take in an animal? Left unresolved, and distinct from Ze'eiri's 30-day post-discharge infertility rule

callout.label: Practical stakes:
callout.text: Getting the definition right determines whether an owner may treat a future birth as certainly non-sacred.

slides.title: 🛒 Buying an Animal From a Fellow Jew
slides.subtitle: Three views on an animal purchased from another Jew, with unknown birth history

lines.speaker: Rav
lines.text: Its offspring is certainly a firstborn. If the seller's animal had already given birth, he would have boasted about it to reassure the buyer.

lines.speaker: Shmuel
lines.text: Its status is uncertain. The seller assumes the buyer wants the animal for slaughter, so he wouldn't bother mentioning its birth history either way.

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: Its offspring is certainly non-sacred. If the animal had not yet given birth, the seller — knowing a prohibition is involved — would surely have informed the buyer.

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: A baraita about slaughtering a mother and offspring together supports Rabbi Yoḥanan's logic: if the seller didn't warn the buyer, he may slaughter freely. Doesn't this refute Rav and Shmuel?

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: No — there, the duty to inform rests on the seller. Here, the duty to inquire rests on the buyer. The two cases allocate responsibility differently.

callout.label: Key difference from the gentile case:
callout.text: A fellow Jew is assumed to follow social norms of disclosure that a gentile seller is not assumed to follow.

slides.title: 🩸 A Mass of Congealed Blood
slides.subtitle: New mishna: Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov on an unusual expulsion

nodes.content: ❓ A large animal expels a mass of congealed blood (חֲרָרַת דָּם) — what is its status?

⚖️ Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov: it must be buried — perhaps a male fetus was consecrated as firstborn within it when it emerged — and the mother is exempt from having any future offspring counted firstborn
🔍 Gemara challenge (Rabbi Ḥiyya): the mass does not impart ritual impurity through touching or carrying, unlike an actual fetus
❔ If it isn't treated as a real fetus for impurity, why must it still be buried? An open question as the daf continues

callout.label: Underlying logic:
callout.text: Burial expresses doubt about sanctity even where the mass fails the standard test for being a fetus.

summary.principle: Every uncertainty about a birth — whether about timing, the nature of a discharge, a seller's silence, or an unusual expulsion — is resolved through carefully isolated technical distinctions rather than blanket assumptions.

flowSteps.content: 🐐 A fourth explanation completes the tanna kama/Rabbi Shimon dispute: can a too-young animal enter the tithe pen?
📜 That halakha itself traces to a verbal analogy, not a resemblance to either firstborns or sacrifices
🩸 A murky discharge is defined precisely (Rava vs. Shmuel), with fetal-formation timing left open

columns.content: 🛒 Buying from a Jew: three views (Rav, Shmuel, Rabbi Yoḥanan) on who bears the duty to disclose or inquire
🩸 New mishna: a mass of congealed blood must be buried on doubt alone, despite failing the impurity test for a fetus

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Uncertainty in firstborn law is managed through precise definitions and burden-of-proof rules, not by default assumptions

quiz.q: What is the fourth explanation the Gemara offers for the dispute between the baraita's first tanna and Rabbi Shimon regarding the goat's triplets reaching the tithe quota?
o: Whether goats can bear more than three offspring
Whether an animal too young to be sacrificed (מְחוּסַּר זְמַן) may enter the pen to be tithed
Whether the tithe applies to female animals at all
Whether Ze'eiri's rule applies to sheep as well as goats
quiz.e: The fourth explanation holds that all previous distinctions are agreed upon, and the real dispute is whether an animal too young to be sacrificed can nonetheless enter the pen to be counted for the animal tithe.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's conclusion, what is the actual source for the rule that a mechusar zman animal enters the tithe pen?
o: A direct comparison of traits shared with ordinary sacrifices
A direct comparison of traits shared with the firstborn
A verbal analogy between 'you shall pass' (firstborn) and 'passes under the rod' (tithe)
There is no textual source; it is a rabbinic enactment
quiz.e: After testing and rejecting comparisons based on shared traits with either firstborns or sacrifices, the Gemara concludes that Rabbi Shimon derives the halakha from a verbal analogy (גְּזֵרָה שָׁוָה) between the terms used for firstborn and tithe.

quiz.q: According to Rava (citing what shepherds say), what is a 'murky discharge' that exempts a future offspring from firstborn status?
o: Bubbles of blood
A discharge indicating the animal absorbed or suppressed a fetus in the womb
Ordinary afterbirth from a completed pregnancy
A discharge that only occurs after the animal's first year
quiz.e: Rava, citing the way shepherds describe it, defines the murky discharge as an indicator that the animal suppressed or absorbed a fetus within its womb; Shmuel instead defines it as bubbles of blood.

quiz.q: Why does Rabbi Yoḥanan hold that the offspring of an animal purchased from a fellow Jew is certainly non-sacred (definitely not a firstborn)?
o: Because Jewish sellers never sell pregnant animals
Because if the animal had not yet given birth, the seller — aware of the prohibition involved — would surely have informed the buyer
Because firstborn status only applies to animals purchased from gentiles
Because Rabbi Yoḥanan rejects the concept of firstborn sanctity
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan reasons that since a real prohibition is at stake, a Jewish seller would certainly have disclosed if the animal had not yet given birth — so silence implies it must have already given birth, making any future offspring non-sacred.

quiz.q: Why does Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov rule that a mass of congealed blood expelled by a large animal must be buried?
o: Because it definitely contains ritual impurity
Because it might have contained a male fetus that was consecrated as a firstborn when it emerged
Because all blood expelled by an animal must be buried by Torah law
Because it disqualifies the mother from ever giving birth again
quiz.e: Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov's concern is that the mass might have contained a male fetus that attained firstborn consecration upon emerging, so out of doubt it must be buried, even though the mother becomes exempt from having a future offspring counted firstborn.
